processing: A baked green: fixed, cooled, then given a first and a second baking, without heavy shaping, so the leaf keeps a loose flower-like form.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Zhejiang famous greens.
appearance_dry: Loose, curled, jade-green leaves that together suggest a peony beginning to open.
appearance_liquor: Clear, bright pale green, as is typical of fresh baked greens.
appearance_wet: Tender green shoots that open softly in the water.
taste_profile: Fresh and brisk with a returning sweetness; descriptions mention a chestnut note and a light orchid-like floral scent.

brewing.notes: Glass shows the shape. Keep the water below a boil so the floral note stays.

vintage_note: As with other Zhejiang greens it is sold as the current spring harvest and is best within a year. Protected origin covers 14 townships in Jiangshan, so look for that city on the pack. It mostly goes to domestic city markets, with a little exported.
description:
Jiangshan Lü Mudan, 'Jiangshan green peony', comes from the Xianxia range in Jiangshan, at the southwest corner of Zhejiang. Its name is a promise about looks: the leaf is meant to resemble a green peony.

The process is a light one: fix the leaf, let it cool, then bake it twice. Baking rather than wok-pressing lets the leaf keep a soft, open shape, and that shape is what the tea is sold on.

In the cup it is fresh and brisk with a sweet return. Descriptions mention chestnut and a quiet floral scent, a combination common in good Zhejiang spring greens. Water just below 85 C and a glass will do it justice.

It sells mainly in Shanghai, Beijing and Hangzhou, with small amounts going to Singapore and Germany, so finding it abroad takes some effort. It is an appellation tea, so check for the place on the pack, along with the current year's spring date.
history:
The tea was known earlier as Xianxia tea or Xianxia Hualong. Local accounts link it to a poem said to be by Su Dongpo thanking a friend for tea from Xianxia and to a story of a Ming emperor, and they describe it as Song tribute later lost; treat the stories as local tradition.

The modern tea is a revival from 1980, when tea technicians at the county's local products company worked in Bao'an township to recreate it and gave it the present name. It is now a Chinese geographical indication product.
